built.changed:
Added a full pause/settings layer to doc-1.html, keyed on Escape:

1. Escape opens/closes an HTML overlay menu (`#pauseOverlay`) styled to match the game's theme, positioned over the `.shell` (added `position: relative` to `.shell` and a `.pause-overlay`/`.pause-panel`/`.pause-menu` CSS block). Menu items: Resume, Mute Music / Unmute Music, Mute SFX / Unmute SFX, Enable Visuals / Disable Visuals, Restart, Quit — navigable with ArrowUp/ArrowDown, activated with Enter/Space, and also clickable with the mouse. Labels update live to reflect current toggle state.

2. The pause genuinely halts the simulation: `loop()` now skips both `updateParticles(dt)` and the entire gravity/lock/input-repeat block whenever `paused` is true, so the board freezes exactly as left (no gravity ticks, no particle drift) instead of just being visually covered. On resume (`closeMenu()`), `last` and `lockStart` are reset to `now()` so an arbitrarily long pause doesn't cause a snap-drop or steal the lock-delay window; `heldDir`/`dasActive` are cleared on pause entry so DAS doesn't resume as if a key were still held.

3. Mute Music / Mute SFX are independent toggles. Added a real music system to give "Mute Music" something to mute: a quiet 4-note bass loop (`MUSIC_NOTES`, `musicTick()`, `setInterval(musicTick, 480)`) built on the existing `beep()` synth, gated on `!musicMuted && !paused && !over`. The four existing SFX functions (`playLockSound`, `playLineClearSound`, `playLevelUpSound`, `playGameOverSound`) now early-return when `sfxMuted`.

4. Enable/Disable Visuals gates the particle burst (`spawnParticles`), screen shake (`triggerShake`), and lock-flash (in `lockPiece`) behind `visualsEnabled`; core rendering (grid, ghost piece, board, HUD) is untouched.

5. Persisted best score: `best` is read from `localStorage.getItem('tetris-best')` at load, shown in a new "Best" HUD stat between Score and Level, and updated/persisted via `localStorage.setItem` the moment `score` exceeds it inside `lockPiece()`. It survives `reset()` (never zeroed by restart) so it persists across in-session restarts and across page reloads.

6. Quit ends the current run by setting `over = true` (reusing the existing Game-Over overlay and "press any key to restart" flow) without playing the game-over sting, since it's a deliberate action rather than a failure.

7. Added `<kbd>Esc</kbd> Pause` to the on-screen controls list for discoverability (removed from the prose hint where it had briefly been, kept it only in the controls row to avoid duplicating the same fact in two places).

gaps_in_order: core-mechanics-rules round 1: B's lockPiece() silently discards any piece cell that ends up above row 0 at lock time (`if (piece.y + r >= 0) board[...] = piece.c` with no else branch) instead of ending the game, so a piece that locks partially off the top of the board vanishes in part and the game keeps running with `over` still false — confirmed by directly reproducing the state and calling the real lockPiece(). A's lockPiece() has an explicit `if (ny < 0) { triggerGameOver(); return; }` guard on the same code path and does not have this failure.

core-mechanics-rules round 2: doc-1's game-over is a dead end: `addEventListener('keydown', e => { if (over) return; ... })` never resets `over`, and no other code rebuilds `board`/`score` — so after any top-out the game cannot be played again without reloading the page. Combined with having no level or lines-cleared state at all (only a score integer), this is the single largest hole relative to doc-2, which shows a GAME OVER overlay with final score and restarts correctly on any keypress, and tracks/display level and lines throughout.

core-mechanics-rules round 3: B has no next-piece preview, no hold queue, and no ghost/landing-preview at all — the player gets zero foresight into what is coming or where the current piece will land, which is baseline functionality in every modern shipped Tetris (including the winner). That single absence, more than any cosmetic difference, is what makes B read as a stripped-down mechanics demo rather than a finished game.

core-mechanics-rules round 4: doc-1 gives zero audio or visual payoff for any game event — locking a piece, clearing a line (even a 4-line Tetris), leveling up, or topping out all render as an instant, silent, flat re-paint of the canvas with no sound, no particle/flash, and no screen reaction. doc-2 plays a line-clear sound, spawns particles per cleared row, and triggers a screen-shake on a Tetris. Concretely: open both, clear a line in each — doc-1's board just silently redraws one row shorter; doc-2's fires playLineClearSound() plus spawnParticles() (and triggerSlamShake() for a 4-line clear). That absence is what makes doc-1 read as a correct engine rather than a shipped game.

core-mechanics-rules round 5: B has essentially no presentation layer: default black background, unstyled system-font text for score/level/lines, an unbordered/gridless play canvas, and a raw paragraph of instructions where A has a menu system — there is no panel/card chrome, no visual hierarchy, and nothing that signals "shipped game" rather than "engine test page." That is the single largest thing standing between B and A: not rule-correctness (which is close to tied) but the total absence of the UI/visual layer the goal explicitly demands ("nothing in it should read as a prototype").

core-mechanics-rules round 6: Doc-1 has no pause/settings layer at all: no way to mute audio, no way to safely step away without losing the run, no persisted best score across restarts. Doc-2 has a fully working Escape-triggered menu (Resume/Mute Music/Mute SFX/Enable Visuals/Restart/Quit) that genuinely halts the simulation while paused; doc-1 has nothing bound to Escape and no equivalent surface at all. That is the single largest completeness gap between them.

core-mechanics-rules round 7: B (doc-1.html) has no pre-game starting-level selector and no alternate keybind scheme: every game is forced to begin at level 1 (dropMs 700) with arrow-keys-only control, whereas A lets the player pick a starting level before the first piece spawns and offers WASD/Z/X/C/Shift as full alternates to the arrow set — a concrete leveling/accessibility surface B simply does not expose.

core-mechanics-rules round 8: doc-1's piece spawner uses uniform `Math.random()` per slot with no bag (`fillQueue(){ while(queue.length<NEXT_COUNT) queue.push(Math.floor(Math.random()*SHAPES.length)) }`), so it can legally deal the same piece many times in a row or withhold a type (e.g. no I-piece) for dozens of spawns — a real, guideline-violating fairness defect in the rules layer. Fix: replace it with a shuffled-bag generator like doc-2's `shuffledBag()/nextPiece()` (each of the 7 types exactly once per bag, reshuffle when exhausted).

core-mechanics-rules round 9: doc-2's own displayed score (left panel "Score: 290") disagrees with the score reported in its own GAME OVER modal ("292") in the same rendered frame — the same underlying score value is shown two different ways at the single moment a player needs it to be authoritative. Fix: route both readouts from one state update in the same tick so panel and modal always agree, verified by asserting `scorePanel.textContent === gameOverModal.scoreText` at the frame game-over triggers.

core-mechanics-rules round 10: A ships with zero <audio> elements (document.querySelectorAll('audio').length === 0) — the game is completely silent, no line-clear/drop/game-over sound feedback at all — whereas B has a background-music track and a dedicated line-clear sound effect wired up (confirmed present and attempting to play, gated only by the standard browser autoplay-gesture rule). For an artifact whose bar is "shipped and kept working on... how it feels under the hand," a totally silent game reads as an unfinished channel, and this is the single largest concretely-verified difference between the two once core mechanics are already a tie.

core-mechanics-rules round 11: B's scoring model omits hard-drop and soft-drop distance bonuses entirely — `score += [0,100,300,500,800][cleared] * level` is the only place score changes in the whole file, so a player who plays efficiently (hard-dropping instead of waiting on gravity) earns exactly the same score as one who does nothing but wait, which is a real deviation from the standard scoring rules that A correctly implements (LINE_SCORES plus HARD_DROP_SCORE=2/row and SOFT_DROP_SCORE=1/row, both confirmed firing in real play).

core-mechanics-rules round 12: doc-2's hard-drop/gravity collision resolution can lock a piece into the board with fully empty, unsupported columns beneath it — reproduced twice (a horizontal I-piece at board row 12 over columns 6-9, and another at row 13 over columns 3-6, with rows 13-19 confirmed empty in those same columns via averaged pixel sampling and a screenshot). A round whose builder reported no snapshot says so in `regression_why_not` rather than reading as a round that was checked and found fine.
Position bias is split across the line within each round, which measures it rather than eliminating it. It is not removed.

The up to 3 critic(s) share a model family and prompt, so their verdicts are not independent judgments; k copies resample one model's habits. Nothing here measures how much independence the line actually supplies, and no arithmetic over k should be read as if it did.

THE SPLIT IS NOT CHECKED. A lead agent chose these 4 piece(s) and nothing verified the choice: its criterion was "The artifact is one self-contained HTML/JS file (confirmed by inspecting doc-2's own code, which itself keeps DAS/ARR constants, SRS rotation+kick tables, canvas/sprite/particle rendering, and pause/settings/game-over overlays as distinct concerns), so the seams are drawn not by file boundaries but by which distinct probe technique judges each concern in isolation: driven-key-sequence state/score inspection for rule correctness, screenshots across states and window sizes for what is seen and communicated, timed key-hold sequences for control feel, and console/session-edge interactions for pause/restart/error-free and single-file robustness.". Each piece was required to name what would be inspected to judge it alone, and pieces that named none were dropped in code — but a plausible observable is not a correct seam. A split drawn around known weaknesses hides them, and every piece can win while the artifact as a whole is worse than the reference. The whole-artifact check that would have noticed did not run: the run never reached WON, so no winning split existed to falsify — this check only runs after every piece has beaten the reference

The goal is operator-supplied, and reads as independent of the candidate. That is a fact about the two texts: nothing here can see when the goal was written or by whom, and a goal written after looking at the candidate can be phrased so that it does not overlap with it.

k>1 is an ADDITION, not source fidelity. Both primary texts hold judges at one per piece — "Each piece gets its own builder and a separate critic with fresh context." — and get width by decomposing the goal — which this loop also does, when a lead returns a usable split. So k is a SECOND axis of width the source never describes: the source multiplies PIECES and holds judges at one, and k multiplies JUDGES within a piece. What k buys is a stronger reading of "every judge satisfied" than one critic can give; what it is not is fidelity, and at the default k=1 that phrase quantifies over a set of one.

AT k=3 THE EXIT IS UNANIMITY OVER 3 JUDGES on the piece(s) the lead raised, and over 1 elsewhere, bought because five judges on one unchanged near-boundary pair split 3-2 (scripts/split-extract.mjs) and a single win can therefore be a coin flip. What k cannot fix is a bias every judge shares: they are spawned from one model family against one prompt, so unanimity narrows variance and not common-mode error. WHO SETS k IS NOT SETTLED BY MEASUREMENT (issue #63): the floor is the operator's — args.critics=1 — the source's own arrangement, "a separate critic with fresh context", singular — and above it only the lead, per piece, with a recorded reason, and only upward; the split ledger's discordance rate is k-free by construction (issue #71) but yields a per-judge error only if a judge is assumed to beat a coin — disagreement cannot tell a good judge from a bad one — so it informs k and does not set it. The lead raised "visual-rendering-hud" to 3 (Whether a HUD, palette, and animation read as 'shipped' versus 'prototype' is a look/feel judgement call — different reviewers will not converge on one pass through it.); "input-feel-responsiveness" to 3 (Control feel (snappy vs. laggy, forgiving vs. punishing) is a judgement call about hand-feel, not a pass/fail measurement, so different critics can reasonably disagree in one pass.). Whether a lead's raise is any better than a fixed number is unmeasured; both numbers are in decomposition.pieces[].critics so a crossing could compare them.

THE SPLIT LEDGER IS FED BY HAND OR NOT AT ALL. Every armed round produces the paired observation that would narrow the choice of k — two independently spawned judges on identical bytes at opposite positions — and the loop cannot record it, having no filesystem. Unless someone runs `node scripts/split-ledger.mjs --ingest <verdict.json>` against this verdict, these trials are discarded and k remains chosen by argument rather than by measurement.
Critic and builder share a model family, so the critic may be blind to exactly the mistakes the builder is prone to making.

THE REFUSAL'S AUTHORITY IS CONDITIONED ON THE CORPUS, NOT ONLY ON YOU (issue #28). The pairing check's GENERATOR verdict stops a run by default because 6 distinct pairings in the false-refusal cell, 18 draws, none falsely refused, none flipped over 6 redrawn — no counterexample on file. That is absence of a counterexample, not evidence of accuracy: the interval on the false-refusal rate reaches 39%, and a probe consistently wrong in the same way passes this test. The numbers are in refusal_authority and are a copy of oracle/results.jsonl as tallied by scripts/oracle-report.mjs, recomputed by the suite; the day the corpus records a false refusal or a flipped verdict, the default becomes a warning without anyone editing this file. What the corpus cannot supply: ground truth nobody authored (#33, #38) — every pairing in it was labelled by a person, so a probe that agrees with its labeller passes.

THE BLINDNESS PROBE MODELS THE FILESYSTEM ONLY, and the critic and builder both hold WebSearch and WebFetch. The probe resolves an artifact's citations against this working tree, so a `clean` verdict means neither artifact gives away its origin TO A READER OF THIS DISK. It says nothing about the network: a reference with a published copy can be fetched and compared, which identifies which side is the shipped one, and a builder can retrieve a fix from the web rather than composing it — a live retrieval channel distinct both from the model's own prior and from anything on disk, and the one issue #25 does not cover. Neither agent needs the network for its stated job.

THE PAIRING CHECK READS THIS DISK TOO, and staging was measured once (#35): the goal-check probe holds Bash and can grep the tree, and its verdicts were drawn on the same six constructed artifacts in-tree and byte-identically staged outside the repository — 6/6 rows unchanged over 30 draws (docs/runs/2026-08-31-blindness-residual/verdict.md). One comparison finding nothing, not proof: six constructed artifacts, one model family, and staging cannot touch what the model recognises from content alone or fetches from the network.

The critic holds Bash and KillShell, which can write files directly (redirection, heredocs, etc.) — nothing mechanically stops it from altering either artifact through Bash instead of Write/Edit. The no-Write/no-Edit property above is real but narrow (prompt-deep, not structural).
AB_SCHEMA.gap is a free-text string: nothing stops several gaps being packed into it (e.g. "Gap 1: ... Gap 2: ..."). Only one gap SLOT is enforced, not one gap.
Nothing verifies that the named gap is really the LARGEST — only that exactly one slot came back.

NO CALIBRATION ANYWHERE. Nothing in this plugin checks that a critic could have failed — no defect is planted, no control is run on a clean copy, and a critic that approves everything is indistinguishable from a critic that is right. The seeded-defect machinery that used to do this lived in the review panel and was deleted with it; this is now the plugin's largest unmeasured property, not a lane that exists elsewhere.

The breaker is checked at ROUND BOUNDARIES, not continuously. Removing the token while a critic or builder is mid-flight does not abort that agent — the run stops before the next round starts. To stop a round already in progress, kill the workflow itself.
Nothing stops the token being re-created after a cancel. The breaker reports the state at each boundary; it does not latch.

With no budget target set, there is no pre-committed ceiling at all — the run continues until it wins, an agent fails, or the operator cancels. That is the source design rather than an oversight — it says "there should be no arbitrary final round" — and it means an unattended run is bounded only by the host's own runaway backstop.

exit_bar.bar: the candidate wins the blind A/B and every critic in the line reports a margin of `clear` or `decisive`. Stated as an allow-list on purpose: a critic that omits the margin or returns a value outside the enum is NOT wowed, so an unreadable answer costs a round rather than ending the run
exit_bar.note: Counts judgements, not correctness. Each is one blind A/B by a separately spawned critic comparing the whole candidate against the whole reference; nothing in this run establishes that any of them could have failed.

split_check.why_not: the run never reached WON, so no winning split existed to falsify — this check only runs after every piece has beaten the reference

reading_note: Stopping on CANCELLED or BUDGET is not failure. The source is explicit that a hard bar "does not need to be realistically reachable" and that the operator stopping is the normal ending — Shumer stopped his own run "while it was still improving". Read `gaps_in_order` instead: if the gaps got smaller and more specific, the loop was working. If the last round names the same gap as the first, it was not — and that is the signal to read, not the verdict. Then read `goal_coverage`: gaps sharpen only inside the pieces that ran, and a drill that sharpened for five rounds says nothing about a clause no piece cited or one that sat in a piece that never ran a round (issue #67).
